explanation.value: Since $$u(2t)=u(t)$$ for positive scaling, let $$x(t)=e^{-t}u(t).$$ Then $$x(2t)=e^{-2t}u(2t).$$ Using the time-scaling property, $$\mathcal{L}\{x(at)\}=\dfrac{1}{a}X\left(\dfrac{s}{a}\right),\;a>0.$$ Hence $$\mathcal{L}\{e^{-2t}u(2t)\}=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\frac{s}{2}+1}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{s+2}}.$$

q.value: The unilateral Laplace transform of a signal is $$X(s)=\dfrac{s+6}{s(s+2)(s+3)}.$$ The value of $$x(0^+)+x(\infty)$$ is:   1 Mark

explanation.value: Using the Initial Value Theorem, $$x(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}sX(s)$$=$$\lim_{s\to\infty}\frac{s(s+6)}{s(s+2)(s+3)}=0.$$ Using the Final Value Theorem, since all poles of $$sX(s)=\dfrac{s+6}{(s+2)(s+3)}$$ lie in the left-half plane, $$x(\infty)=\lim_{s\to0}sX(s)=\frac{6}{(2)(3)}=1.$$ Therefore, $$x(0^+)+x(\infty)=0+1=\boxed{1}.$$

Using the multiplication-by-$n$ property, $$\mathcal{Z}\{n x[n]\}=-z\dfrac{dX(z)}{dz}.$$ Here $$X(z)=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}.$$ Differentiating, $$\dfrac{dX(z)}{dz}=-\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}z^{-2}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}\right)^2}.$$ Hence, $$\mathcal{Z}\{n x[n]\}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}\right)^2}.$$ Therefore, the correct answer is $$\boxed{\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}\right)^2}}.$$

q.value: If bilateral Z-transform $$\mathcal{Z}\{x[n]\}=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}},$$ then $$\mathcal{Z}\{x[n-2]\}$$ is:   1 Mark

explanation.value: Using the time-shifting property for the bilateral Z-transform, $$x[n-k]\Longleftrightarrow z^{-k}X(z).$$ For $$k=2,$$ we get $$\mathcal{Z}\{x[n-2]\}=z^{-2}X(z).$$ Hence, $$\mathcal{Z}\{x[n-2]\}=\dfrac{z^{-2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}.$$ Therefore, the correct answer is $$\boxed{\dfrac{z^{-2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}}.$$

q.value: For a causal discrete-time signal, the Z-transform is $$X(z)=\dfrac{z}{(z-1)(z-\frac{1}{2})}.$$ The value of $$x[0]+x[\infty]$$ is:   1 Marks

explanation.value: Using the Initial Value Theorem, $$x[0]=\lim_{z\to\infty}X(z)$$$$=\lim_{z\to\infty}\dfrac{z}{(z-1)(z-\frac{1}{2})}=0.$$ For the Final Value Theorem, $$x[\infty]=\lim_{z\to1}(1-z^{-1})X(z).$$ The pole at z=1 is removed by the factor $(1-z^{-1})$, and the remaining pole at $$z=\frac{1}{2}$$ lies inside the unit circle. Therefore, the Final Value Theorem is applicable. Hence, $x[\infty]=\lim_{z\to1}\left(1-z^{-1}\right)\dfrac{z}{(z-1)(z-\frac{1}{2})}$=$\lim_{z\to1}\dfrac{1}{z-\frac{1}{2}}=2.$ Therefore, $$x[0]+x[\infty]=0+2=\boxed{2}.$$

q.value: The Z-transform of a discrete-time signal is $$X(z)=\dfrac{1}{(1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1})(1-2z^{-1})}.$$ For which ROC does the corresponding signal have a DTFT?   1 Marks

explanation.value: The DTFT exists if the unit circle $$|z|=1$$ lies within the ROC of the Z-transform. The poles are at $$z=\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$z=2.$$ Therefore, the possible ROCs are $$|z|>2,$$ $$|z|<\frac{1}{2},$$ and $$\frac{1}{2}<|z|<2.$$ Only $$\frac{1}{2}<|z|<2$$ contains the unit circle $$|z|=1$$. Hence, the corresponding signal has a DTFT only for $$\boxed{\frac{1}{2}<|z|<2}.$$

q.value:
Match List-I with List-II.   1 Marks

List-I: Signal
(P) Continuous-time periodic signal
(Q) Continuous-time non-periodic signal
(R) Discrete-time periodic signal
(S) Discrete-time non-periodic signal

List-II: Spectrum
(1) Discrete and periodic
(2) Continuous and non-periodic
(3) Discrete and non-periodic
(4) Continuous and periodic

explanation.value: For a continuous-time periodic signal, the Fourier series representation gives a discrete spectrum, which is generally non-periodic. A continuous-time non-periodic signal has a continuous and non-periodic spectrum. A discrete-time periodic signal has a discrete and periodic spectrum. For a discrete-time non-periodic signal, the DTFT is continuous and periodic. Therefore, the correct matching is $$\boxed{(P)\text{–}(3),\ (Q)\text{–}(2),\ (R)\text{–}(1),\ (S)\text{–}(4)}.$$

q.value: Consider the discrete-time signal $$x[n]=1,\quad -4\le n\le4,$$ and $$x[n]=0,otherwise.$$ The DTFT $$X(e^{j\omega})$$ of this signal is:   2 Mark

explanation.value: The DTFT is $$X(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=-4}^{4}e^{-j\omega n}.$$ Since the signal is symmetric about $$n=0$$, $$X(e^{j\omega})=1+2\sum_{n=1}^{4}\cos(n\omega).$$ Using the standard finite-sum result, $$1+2\sum_{n=1}^{4}\cos(n\omega)=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{9\omega}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)}.$$ Hence, $$\boxed{X(e^{j\omega})=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{9\omega}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)}}.$$

q.value: A periodic half-wave rectified cosine signal is defined as $$x(t)=\begin{cases}\cos t,&0\le t\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\0,&\dfrac{\pi}{2}<t\le\pi\end{cases}$$ and is repeated with period $$T=\pi.$$ The Laplace transform $$X(s)$$ is:   2 Mark

explanation.value: Using the Laplace transform property for periodic signals, $$X(s)=\dfrac{F_1(s)}{1-e^{-sT}},$$ where $T=\pi$ and $$F_1(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{\cos t\left[u(t)-u\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]\right\}.$$ Now, $$F_1(s)=\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-st}\cos t\,dt=\dfrac{s+e^{-\pi s/2}}{s^2+1}.$$ Hence, $$X(s)=\dfrac{s+e^{-\pi s/2}}{(s^2+1)(1-e^{-\pi s})}.$$
